metadata.file_name: The mediating moderating model of inquiry-based learning and science self-efficacy  evidence from PISA 2015.pdf
metadata.title: The mediating–moderating model of inquiry-based learning and science self-efficacy: evidence from PISA 2015

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata from 57 participating countries and economies, with a two-stage stratified sampling design (schools selected with PPS, then students selected with equal probability within schools). The authors report that PISA constructs for the focal latent variables were scaled using IRT and that WLE scores were used as individual student scores, which is consistent with PISA’s scaling approach but does not explicitly state whether complex survey sampling weights were applied in the mediation/moderation regressions. The analysis is conducted in SPSS using the PROCESS macro, which typically performs standard regression/bootstrapping without automatically incorporating PISA replicate-weight variance estimation unless weights are explicitly specified. Because the manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling weights (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT) or replicate weights, readers should treat the reported standard errors and confidence intervals as model-based rather than fully design-based.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables (science self-efficacy, science interest, teacher support) are reported as WLE scores derived from IRT scaling of questionnaire items, and the paper does not describe any additional missing-data procedure for the analytic variables. This is a reporting gap: PISA datasets typically include item nonresponse, and mediation/moderation estimates depend on how missing responses were handled (e.g., imputation vs. complete-case rules). Without documentation, the robustness of the mediation/moderation coefficients to missingness cannot be evaluated.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 student data for 15-year-olds from 57 participating countries and economies, restricted to cases where students had administered questions measuring all variables of interest in the PISA 2015 context questionnaires (inquiry-based science teaching and learning practices, science interest, science self-efficacy, teacher support in science classes of students’ choice) plus the control variables (gender and disciplinary climate in science classes). The analytic sample therefore excludes students who did not have responses enabling computation of the required WLE-based scores for all focal constructs.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) Science — inquiry-based learning (IBTEACH) → science self-efficacy (SCIEEFF) with science interest (INTBRSCI) mediation
main_findings.performance_metrics: Mediation (PROCESS Model 4; 5,000 bootstrap samples; standardized coefficients): total effect B=0.194 (p<.001), direct effect B=0.155 (p<.001), indirect effect B=0.039 (95% CI [0.038, 0.040]); R2 for science self-efficacy model=0.045; F(3)=5383.545 (p<.001). Relative effects: direct 79.9%, indirect 20.1%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science the study leveraged inquiry-based learning, science interest, and controls (gender and disciplinary climate) to predict science self-efficacy, finding that inquiry-based learning had a significant positive direct effect and a partially mediated indirect effect through science interest (indirect effect accounting for 20.1% of the total effect). This indicates that strengthening inquiry-based learning may improve students’ science self-efficacy partly by fostering science interest, suggesting that science instruction should be designed to build both engagement and confidence, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) Science — moderated mediation with teacher support (TEACHSUP)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Moderated mediation (PROCESS Model 59; 5,000 bootstrap samples; standardized coefficients): inquiry-based learning × teacher support interaction predicting science self-efficacy B=0.049 (p<.001); science interest × teacher support interaction B=-0.015 (p<.001). Direct effect by teacher support levels: low (M−SD) B=0.087, mean (M) B=0.136, high (M+SD) B=0.185. Indirect effect by teacher support levels: low B=0.034, mean B=0.028, high B=0.021. R2 for science self-efficacy model=0.111; F(7)=6183.459 (p<.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science the study leveraged inquiry-based learning, teacher support, science interest, and controls (gender and disciplinary climate) to predict science self-efficacy in a moderated mediation framework, finding that teacher support positively moderated the direct effect of inquiry-based learning but negatively moderated the indirect pathway via science interest (indirect effect decreased from 0.034 to 0.021 as teacher support increased). This indicates that teacher support can amplify the confidence-building impact of inquiry-based learning directly, while simultaneously weakening the extent to which science interest mediates that effect, implying that teacher practices should be calibrated to preserve student autonomy and interest while providing effective scaffolding.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) Science data from 57 participating countries and economies (N=346,109) to test a mediating–moderating model linking inquiry-based learning to science self-efficacy. Using WLE-scaled PISA questionnaire constructs—science self-efficacy (SCIEEFF) as the outcome, inquiry-based learning (IBTEACH) as the predictor, science interest (INTBRSCI) as the mediator, and teacher support (TEACHSUP) as the moderator—authors estimate mediation and moderated mediation with PROCESS in SPSS using 5,000 bootstrap samples. Results show a significant positive total effect (B=0.194, p<.001) with partial mediation: the indirect effect via science interest is B=0.039, representing 20.1% of the total effect. Teacher support strengthens the direct effect (direct effect rises from 0.087 to 0.185 from low to high teacher support) but reduces the indirect effect (from 0.034 to 0.021). The paper reports correlations/standardized regression coefficients rather than causal effects, and it does not document missing-data handling or whether PISA complex survey weights were applied in the estimation.
